A Burndown Chart is a graphical representation to track work completed by the team against the work planned for a given sprint. The graph displays all of the work planned as well as remaining (Y axis) on any given day of the sprint (X axis). The chart will show less and less work remaining as the team progresses and completes work. The chart empowers the team to own and visualize the plan thereby allowing them to manage any difficulties earlier and more decisively.

The Burndown Chart also has a line to represent the "ideal burndown". This indicates the ideal scenario where work would be completed at a uniform pace throughout the course of the sprint. Once the sprint is complete, the Burndown Chart is a catalog of patterns on observed performance. Compiled over time the Burndown Charts become an extensive history of past performance.

The chart contains information on the:

  1. Dynamics of the sprint - such as the pace of work, discoveries made and the impact of adding work to the sprint in the case where the team is running ahead of schedule
  2. Current progress - toward achieving the goal outlined for the sprint
  3. Need to adjust - such as changes to the sprint goal or removing impediments to speed up progress

Finally, progress for an entire release can also be documented and tracked via a Burndown Chart at the release level. The key differences between sprint and release level Burndown Charts are as follows:

Sprint Burndown Chart Release Burndown Chart
X axis Days # of Sprints
Y axis
  • Story points sum,
  • Ideal Days, or
  • # of Tasks
  • Story points sum,
  • Ideal Days, or
  • # of Backlog Items
Update Frequency As work is completed or at least daily Updated once per sprint, at the end
Inputs Sprint Backlog estimates Product Backlog estimates

The Burndown Chart:

  • Does not indicate scope changes to items
  • Can provide insight on trends such as progress of work but does not provide details on partially complete work items
  • Cannot calculate expected cost or budget overruns but can indicate the trajectory of the team
  • Can be maintained in a digital format for ease of collaboration and communication
  • Should be updated as soon as work is completed, this is done automatically if using an Agile tracking tool, or at a minimum during the daily scrum meeting for sprint level Burndown Charts
    • An outdated Burndown Chart can prevent the team from understanding their actual progress against ideal burndown, which ultimately informs the team whether they are on track for the current sprint
    • Release level Burndown Charts need only be updated once per sprint, at the end
To track and monitor progress of the team against the work committed to for a given sprint as well as inform retrospectives.

Without this work product it is:

  • Difficult to monitor daily progress in a given sprint
  • Difficult to mitigate the risk of not completing the remaining work in a sprint

The X axis details time typically expressed in daily intervals starting with the first day of the sprint and ending on the last day of the sprint. Meanwhile, the Y axis depicts planned work remaining which can be expressed via any of the following (depending upon team/project standards):

  • Sum of story point estimates - represents the estimated level of effort in terms of story point summed across all work items in the sprint
  • Sum of hour estimates - represents the estimated level of effort in terms of hours summed across all work items for the sprint
  • Number of tasks - represents the tasks necessary to complete all of the work items for the sprint

1. Digitally - The chart can be maintained digitally via any number of Agile tools which have the capability to generate and maintain Burndown Charts (Rally, Rational Team Concert, Version One, JIRA, etc.).
  2. Manually - The chart, in its simplest form, can be maintained on a piece of paper hung in the team's working area. Alternatively, it can be manually updated via a spreadsheet.

Regardless of the means by which the chart is maintained, it can be displayed in a variety of forms to varying levels of detail:

  • Sprint Burndown Chart via any of the following units of measure:
    • Total effort remaining in hours
    • Story point estimates of Backlog items completed
  • Release Burndown Chart
